title: Every letter differs. How far apart?
hook: FLAW and LAWN clash at all 4 spots.

knows: filling a grid from its neighbours (blocked-cell-routes)
doesNotKnow: how a spell checker measures how different two words are
that the distance between whole words is built from distances between their beginnings

misconception: Two words differ by the number of positions where their letters differ.
objective: The learner can fill the edit-distance grid for FLAW and LAWN (each cell the cheapest of three neighbours plus one, or the diagonal free on a match), read 2 at the corner, and explain why that beats counting mismatched positions (4).

claims.text: FLAW and LAWN differ at all 4 positions.
claims.source: F/L, L/A, A/W, W/N: no position matches. Builder's node check: 4 mismatched positions. Unverified.

claims.text: Turning FLAW into LAWN takes 2 edits: delete F, keep L, A, W, insert N.
claims.source: Builder's node: Levenshtein DP gives 2, and a breadth-first search over single-letter insert/delete/replace edits also reaches LAWN in 2 (KITTEN to SITTING = 3 as a control). The traced path on the stage is delete F, keep L A W, insert N. Unverified.

claims.text: Each grid cell is the cheapest of its three neighbours (above, left, diagonal) plus one, or the diagonal copied free when the two letters match.
claims.source: Wagner and Fischer 1974, 'The string-to-string correction problem', JACM 21(1); CLRS 3rd ed. problem 15-5 (4th ed. 14-5). Builder re-ran the recurrence in node: grid rows 0 1 2 3 4 / 1 1 2 3 4 / 2 1 2 3 4 / 3 2 1 2 3 / 4 3 2 1 2. Reference only: TheAlgorithms/Python strings/levenshtein_distance.py (no code copied). Unverified.

claims.text: Counting spot by spot gives 4, because it never lets letters slide; one delete shifts LAW into line.
claims.source: After deleting F, FLAW becomes LAW, which sits at LAWN's first three positions; only N is then missing. Unverified.

claims.text: Every cell compared two beginnings. The corner said "FLAW → LAWN = 2: insert N (+1), after FLAW → LAW (1)": the whole-word distance was built from a beginning you had already filled, as every cell was, by the cheapest of three neighbours. A small grid replaces trying every sequence of edits.
claims.source: Same recurrence as c3: cell (i, j) is the distance between the first i letters of FLAW and the first j letters of LAWN. Unverified. | REVISED v3 2026-10-14 (demo-builder, wave D r5): Reveal now points at the corner cell's caption (seen by every learner, since the gate requires a full grid) instead of telling 'built from beginnings' with nothing on stage. Corner caption is computed by caption(R, C) from the same table the grid shows. | FC pass 22 (fact-checker, 2026-10-14): own copy of the D/FROM table and caption() (scratchpad fc22/flaw.mjs): corner caption 'FLAW → LAWN = 2: insert N (+1), after FLAW → LAW (1)', matching the reveal (CORNER strips the final period). Every one of the 25 cells equals an independent Levenshtein distance of the two prefixes.

claims.text: The 16 cells the learner fills are the inner cells of a 5 x 5 grid.
claims.source: (4 + 1) x (4 + 1) = 25 cells; the first row and column (9 cells) are given, 25 - 9 = 16. Unverified.

claims.text: Spell checkers and DNA alignment fill this grid.
claims.source: Edit distance in spelling correction: Jurafsky and Martin, Speech and Language Processing, ch. 2 (minimum edit distance); DNA alignment uses the same grid idea (Needleman and Wunsch 1970, J. Mol. Biol. 48; Smith-Waterman). Wording 'fill this grid' is loose: they fill grids of the same kind. Unverified; checker should weigh the wording.

claims.text: Stage legend: ↓ delete · → insert · ↘ replace (free if letters match).
claims.source: Standard Wagner-Fischer reading with the first word down the side: a step down consumes a letter of FLAW (delete), right adds a letter of LAWN (insert), diagonal replaces one with the other at cost 1, or costs 0 when they match. Wagner & Fischer 1974, J. ACM 21(1); Jurafsky & Martin, Speech and Language Processing, 3rd ed. draft, ch. 2 (minimum edit distance). | REVISED v3 2026-10-14 (demo-builder, wave D r5): new sentence. Added for r5 top finding: grid directions had no edit meaning on stage. | FC pass 22 (fact-checker, 2026-10-14): rows are FLAW, columns LAWN: down = consume a FLAW letter (delete), right = add a LAWN letter (insert), diagonal = replace or free match; legend text in the SVG matches. Wagner & Fischer not opened (memory); reading confirmed by derivation.

claims.text: Each cell's caption reads '<beginning of FLAW> → <beginning of LAWN> = n: <edit> (+1 or +0), after <smaller pair> (n')', e.g. 'FL → L = 1: L = L, keep it free (+0), after F → · (1)'. A cell's number is the fewest edits from that beginning of FLAW to that beginning of LAWN.
claims.source: caption() in Demo.tsx; D[i][j] = fewest edits from the first i letters of FLAW to the first j of LAWN (the table comment). All 16 captions printed by a builder node script reproducing Demo.tsx; e.g. FLA → LAW = 2: insert W, after FLA → LA (1). | REVISED v3 2026-10-14 (demo-builder, wave D r5): new sentence. Replaces the per-cell 'cheapest neighbour is diagonal (0 + 1 = 1)' caption. | FC pass 22 (fact-checker, 2026-10-14): all 16 captions printed by my script; format matches; 'FL → L = 1: L = L, keep it free (+0), after F → · (1)' and 'FLA → LAW = 2: insert W (+1), after FLA → LA (1)' reproduced.

recall.question: To fill one cell of the edit-distance grid for two words, which cells do you use?
options: Only the cell to its left
Its three neighbours: above, left and diagonal
recall.why: The cell is the cheapest of the above, left and diagonal neighbours plus one (diagonal free when the letters match), so earlier answers are reused.
